Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-08
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Lina Gomez (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Atlas Head of Platform), Ethan Cole (Atlas ML Infra), Marco Ruiz (Atlas SRE)
Recorded: Zoom (auto-transcript)

Auto-generated summary (optional):
Atlas is evaluating a reserved GPU + burst queue strategy to meet 95/99th tail latency SLOs for a mix of short chat completions and long context batch jobs. They want predictable cost, an on-prem option behind VPC, and a safe autoscaler that avoids cold-cache thrashing. Today we covered queueing models, warmup strategies, KV cache prewarm, batching profiles, and quantization tradeoffs. Action items captured.

Topics:
- Queueing model choices (M/M/c vs hybrid models)
- Burst queue design and latency isolation
- Reserved GPU sizing and safety margins
- KV-cache warmup / prefix caching and eviction policies
- Batching and continuous batching tradeoffs for p99 latency vs throughput
- Low-precision quantization impacts on tail latency and fallbacks
- VPC/on-prem deployment constraints and warmstart strategies

Quick links / refs mentioned: 
- Burst simulator notebook: (link shared in chat) https://redwood.ai/sim/burst-notebook-atlas (placeholder)
- Capacity spreadsheet: /drive/Atlas_capacity_2025Q4.xlsx
- SOC2 + VPC checklist: https://redwood.ai/security/soc2-vpc (short link)

Transcript (timestamps approximate; auto transcript with minor errors):
00:00 Avery: All right everyone, thanks for joining, this is Avery from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. Today Samir and Lina are gonna run the deep dive, aim to get to the nitty-gritty of your burst and reserved GPU plan. Priya, Ethan, Marco, thanks for the time. 
00:18 Priya: Thanks, hi, quick context — we're shipping a conversational robotics operator console, calls are mostly short text completions but we also have large planning prompts that are 8k to 32k tokens. Our SLO is 95th < 180ms for short completions and p99 < 800ms if possible. We're trying to avoid overpaying for idle reserved capacity.
00:40 Samir: Great, that's super helpful. Quick clarifying Q: those p95/p99 SLOs — are they per-token or end-to-end?
00:47 Priya: End-to-end user-perceived, so includes request routing and decode time. Network is pretty stable inside our VPC but we do see bursty spikes during fleet updates.
01:05 Lina: Okay, we also got the traffic histograms Priya sent, looks like a heavy right tail with periodic spikes roughly 2–3 times baseline every 6 hours.
01:18 Ethan: Yep, representative day is attached in the sheet. Most spikes last 2–8 minutes and are correlated with batch planning rollouts to thousands of agents.
01:33 Samir: Perfect. So first principle: for multiple identical GPUs serving requests, classical queueing is M/M/c — but that assumes exponential service time. Our generative workloads have heavy-tailed service time due to variable context lengths and KV cache misses, so M/G/c-ish models are a closer fit.
02:01 Marco: We were hoping to avoid complexity; should we just size high then rely on autoscaling?
02:08 Samir: You'll pay a lot for headroom. Instead we recommend a two-tier design: reserved pool sized for baseline+headroom (e.g., baseline 80% of average load) plus a burst queue backed by either on-demand infra or a small cold pool that can spin up. The trick is to do burst admission control and cache warmup so you don't thrash the KV cache and blow up p99.
02:35 Priya: Explain the admission control piece — is that token-bucket?
02:40 Samir: Token-bucket for ingress shaping is fine, but for internal burst-to-reserved routing, use a dynamic queue with per-customer priority and an estimate of expected service time. We suggested a small predictive admission filter — if expected decode > threshold, route to a separate long-running job pool.
02:58 Avery: And we shared a burst-sim that uses your real histograms to estimate p95/p99 under different policies — that'll be in the notebook.
03:10 Priya: Nice. On KV cache — our current approach is cold-start per shard when model version changes. That kills latency during deployments. Any recommendations?
03:22 Samir: Two options: 1) proactive prewarm using synthetic traffic (prefixes) fed to the serving layer before cutover, or 2) incremental warmstart where the router pins a small percentage of traffic to a canary pool to build KV gradually. For mission-critical low-latency, do both: a quick prewarm + a throttle-canary.
03:46 Ethan: How big is the prewarm cost? If we warm full context for 10k agents that seems expensive.
03:52 Samir: Prewarm only hot prefixes and the KV entries most likely to be used; we use a sliding-window popularity model. In the simulator, a 10% targeted prewarm achieved 70% of warm-hit benefits at ~12% compute cost compared to full prewarm. So you don't need to warm everything.
04:20 Marco: Do we need specialized NVLink topology or can this run on standard DGX-style nodes?
04:27 Lina: For VPC/on-prem we support both; network matters more for multi-GPU KV-sharded serving. If you use model sharding across GPUs, NVLink helps reduce cross-GPU latency. If models are single-GPU, standard 80GB A100 or H100 instances are fine.
04:50 Priya: About batching — our ops team worries batching increases latency for short requests.
04:55 Samir: Continuous batching with latency SLOs is the pattern: you set a max latency cap and the batcher flushes at that cap. For short completions, keep very small max batch size / short flush timers and enable adaptive batching thresholds that shrink when measured p95 climbs.
05:18 Ethan: What about token-level batching vs request-level batching?
05:22 Samir: Token-level batching gives better throughput when decoding long sequences, but it complicates latency accounting. For your mix, use hybrid: request-level batches for short requests and token-level for long running decodes, with separate pools. That isolates tail effects.
05:42 Avery: There's also the cache interplay — large batches reduce per-token overhead but increase chance of cache eviction thrash if many contexts are different. That's why we tune batch window by working set size.
06:00 Priya: Quantization — we ran int8 in prod on a branch, saw some hallucination regressions. Thoughts?
06:07 Lina: Quantization reduces memory & increases throughput but can change SNR of logits. For safety-critical outputs we recommend 1) validate on eval prompts for regressions, 2) use mixed precision for critical layers or fallback to fp16 for any out-of-distribution inputs, and 3) keep a quality-monitoring alert hooked to prompts that you care about.
06:33 Marco: Does quantization impact tail latency? I thought smaller tensors speed things up but might cause more kernel switching overhead?
06:39 Samir: It can. Kernel dispatch costs and some dequant/quant ops add overhead, but the overall lower memory footprint often reduces cache pressure and improves tail for throughput-bound loads. However for tiny requests the additional per-request overhead may dominate; test with your exact workload.
07:00 Priya: You mentioned safety margins for reserved GPU sizing. What's a rule of thumb?
07:06 Samir: We recommend sizing reserved capacity to cover baseline plus a safety buffer correlated to your p95 load — e.g., baseline = median concurrent requests, reserved = baseline * 1.3–1.6 depending on business tolerance. Then allow a burst pool for the right tail. The exact multiplier comes from simulator runs.
07:28 Ethan: Is there a simple queuing metric to watch? CPU-style utilization doesn't capture tail latency.
07:33 Samir: Watch queue length, service time variance, and the estimated waiting time distribution. Also measure KV cache miss rate and cold-start rate. A key derived metric is "effective concurrency" = arrival_rate * mean_service_time; when effective concurrency approaches c (number of servers), tail skyrockets.
07:55 Marco: Got it. On autoscaler behavior — if we autoscale too fast we risk spinning up cold nodes that thrash cache and increase p99; too slow and we drop requests. How do we set cool-downs?
08:07 Samir: Use a conservative scale-up delay combined with a fast preemption of queued bursts: i.e., when a scale-up is triggered, hold a small amount of the queue on pre-warmed helpers or keep a tiny hot standby to soak short spikes. Implement a scale-up policy with a warmup ramp — add nodes in small increments with a per-node warmup timer to avoid immediate routing. Scale-down should be much slower to avoid unnecessary churn.
08:34 Priya: Can Redwood Dedicated hold a small frozen warm pool that's idle but pre-warmed?
08:38 Avery: Yes, Dedicated supports a "warm standby" option: reserved instances that hold cached weights and partial KV to serve instant bursts. There's an additional cost but it can be cheaper than repeated cold starts. We'll share pricing options.
08:54 Ethan: For on-prem — we can't use Redwood's private control-plane for autoscaling. How does the warm-up story change?
08:59 Samir: On-prem you'll likely have a cluster-autoscaler tied to your infra. Approach: keep a small hot pool on-prem and use a hybrid routing policy that falls back to Redwood-hosted burst capacity when on-prem is saturated (policy requires networking and security review). For air-gapped environments you can preplan with larger reserved capacity or bring a dedicated burst hardware appliance.
09:25 Priya: We need to keep everything inside our VPC due to data residency. Is cross-account peering supported?
09:31 Avery: We support VPC peering and PrivateLink-style connectivity. For hybrid bursts we'd negotiate a secure VPN or private link with guaranteed throughput. We also support bringing the control plane inside your VPC for an enterprise license.
09:48 Marco: One of our ops constraints is GPU provisioning time — cold node spin-up is ~7 minutes in our cluster. That kills bursts.
09:55 Lina: That's why reserved + warm standby exists. If your cold spin is slow, rely more on reserved or hybrid cloud bursts. Also consider pre-warmed snapshots and keep a minimal set of nodes ready with model weights loaded.
10:12 Ethan: Some of the math you mentioned earlier — can you go through an example with our numbers?
10:18 Samir: Sure. Using your histogram: baseline concurrent ~ 120, spike peak ~360. Mean service time for short requests ~50ms, but with cache miss it can jump to 400ms. Effective concurrency baseline = 120 * 0.05 = 6, peak = 360 * 0.4 = 144 when many misses — that indicates huge variance. If you only size for baseline concurrency, tail will blow up when miss rate increases. So tighten miss rate via cache prewarm and/or route cache-miss heavy jobs to a separate pool.
11:02 Priya: The numbers show cache miss is the primary driver. How do we instrument to know the miss drivers?
11:07 Samir: Instrument per-prefix KV hit rate, per-model shard miss, per-deployment version miss. Also per-request metadata like context length, token count, and whether the request hit the hot prefix set. We'll send a recommended instrumentation dashboard.
11:24 Marco: Let's talk about queueing discipline — FIFO vs priority. We need to ensure control-plane / operator traffic never starve.
11:31 Samir: Use multi-queue: give operator/control-plane path a dedicated guaranteed lane, then a priority queue for interactive short completions, then a best-effort for long batch planning. Token-bucket shaping at ingress prevents burst floods. Also consider per-route concurrency limits.
11:51 Priya: Is there an existing Redwood autoscaler we can tune?
11:55 Avery: Yes, Redwood Dedicated has autoscaler settings (scale steps, cooldown, warmup timers). For Private deployments we provide an autoscaler blueprint with knobs you can use in your cluster-autoscaler. We'll provide recommended defaults.
12:10 Ethan: About fallback models — you suggested having lightweight smaller models as fallbacks during severe load. What's the typical approach?
12:16 Samir: Keep a quantized 7B or even 3B model variant that can handle low-fidelity requests; route to fallback when latency target would be missed or when cost threshold triggers. Also have a brownout policy that degrades some non-critical features.
12:31 Priya: We worry about quality regressions when falling back. How to signal when fallback is in use?
12:36 Samir: Tag responses with model_version and quality flag. Also feed fallback responses into your eval queue for later analysis. Keep a short-circuit to revert to full model if critical prompts appear.
12:50 Marco: Can we get a simulation that shows fallbacks and their cost/latency tradeoffs?
12:55 Avery: Yes we'll run the simulator with a fallback policy; add that to next steps.
13:05 (short silence)
13:32 Ethan: One more on reserved sizing: if reserved is too large we pay a lot during quiet hours. Any ideas for smoothing cost?
13:38 Samir: Use time-based scheduling for large downtimes (nightly low usage) — scale reserved usage into on-demand if allowed, or use spot instances with fallback. Also negotiate committed usage discounts and daytime-only reserved allocation. The Dedicated product allows reserve blocks that can be rebalanced with burst credits.
14:00 Priya: For on-prem air-gapped, can we have a cold snapshot for rapid restores?
14:06 Lina: Yes, a warm snapshot that includes weights and top-of-KV can be kept on fast storage to reduce load time. Not as fast as fully warm, but much faster than pulling weights from object store.
14:25 Marco: Are there known failure modes? Like cascading evictions?
14:29 Samir: Yes — a common pattern: big spike causes many cache misses, which triggers longer service times, which increases queueing, which increases apparent arrival backlog, causing autoscaler to scale up with cold nodes, increasing misses further. It's a positive feedback loop. Admission control + slow scale-up + warm standbys breaks the loop.
14:53 Priya: What about testing? How do we validate before cutting over?
14:58 Samir: We recommend a staged test: 1) offline simulator with historical traces, 2) shadow traffic to a dedicated test pool, 3) small canary with prewarm then progressive ramp. We'll share a runbook.
15:15 Ethan: Any comments on metrics and alerts?
15:19 Samir: Alert on queue length, p95/p99 latency, KV miss rate, cold-start rate, and drop rate. Also alert on autoscaler churn (node adds/removals per hour). Set multi-threshold alerts so a single metric doesn't trigger escalation unnecessarily.
15:35 Priya: Are there recommended warmup timers?
15:38 Lina: Typical warmup is 30–120s per node depending on model size; for very large models you might need 5–10 minutes but then you'd be in reserved/standby territory. Tune based on observed weight load time and KV refill window.
15:56 Marco: For our mixed workload, what would you actually size as a starting reserved pool?
16:01 Samir: Based on your baseline of 120 concurrent, mean service 50ms with expected 10% miss — I'd suggest reserved to handle ~200 concurrent with 1.4x buffer = 280 concurrency capacity. Convert concurrency to GPUs using per-GPU concurrency (e.g., 60–80 short completions per GPU depending on model/instance). That would be ~4–6 GPUs reserved plus a small warm standby of 1–2 GPUs and a burst pool for spikes. We'll create exact numbers in the spreadsheet.
16:34 Priya: That seems reasonable. Can you also show how to route long planning jobs so they don't block interactive lanes?
16:41 Samir: Route them to a separate long-job pool. Use request tags and route rules in the API gateway. Long jobs can be queued with a longer SLA and different batching strategy optimized for throughput.
16:55 Avery: Quick recap before we open for Qs: we covered queueing model fit, reserve + burst design, cache prewarm strategies, warm standby, batching knobs, quantization caution, fallback models, and autoscaler warmup/cooldown best practices. Next steps: we'll share the simulator, spreadsheet, SOC2/VPC checklist, and a draft 90-day pilot proposal.
17:20 Priya: Quick question — is the burst simulator accurate with versions changes?
17:24 Samir: Simulator can model version rollouts by injecting higher miss rates during cutover windows. We'll run scenarios.
17:33 Ethan: Any gotchas for Kubernetes HPA versus a custom autoscaler?
17:37 Lina: K8s HPA is ok for general scaling but lacks fine-grained warmup and admission control. Many customers pair HPA with a custom controller that orchestrates prewarm steps and routes traffic gradually.
17:52 Marco: Will Redwood's observability show per-token cost breakouts?
17:57 Avery: Yes, Redwood Console shows token-level cost and latency breakdowns, plus model-level dashboards. We'll give you a demo link.
18:09 Priya: Can you remind us about security for hybrid bursts — is KMS allowed cross-account?
18:15 Avery: We can integrate with customer KMS via peerings; for cross-account you can use an HSM-backed approach or a tokenized proxy inside your VPC. We'll include details in the security doc.
18:30 (noise, muffled chatter)
19:02 Ethan: Ok that's probably enough to start. We'll run the simulator and send more traces.
19:06 Priya: Thanks a lot, this was helpful.
19:10 Samir: Thanks — action items: we'll run the latency sims, determine reserved size proposals, and share the runbook & checklist.
19:24 Avery: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with links and calendar for the runbook session.
